**SECTION THREE: TEXTUAL STUDIES / ANALYSIS**

**Sub-Section One: RENÉ DESCARTES: Meditations on First Philosophy**

*Read the following passage and answer the questions below:*

> "It is no surprise that God in creating me should have placed this idea in me, to serve as a mark of the craftsman stamped on his work (not that he needed any mark other than the work itself). But the mere fact that God created me is a good reason for thinking that I am somehow made in his image and likeness, and that I perceive that likeness in the same way that I perceive myself. That is, when I turn my mind's eye upon myself, I understand that I am a thing that is incomplete and dependent on something else, and which aspires without limit to ever greater and better things; but I also understand at the same time that he on whom I depend has within him all those greater things, and hence that he is God. The core of the argument is this: I couldn't exist with the nature that I have that is, containing within me the idea of God if God didn't really exist. By 'God' I mean the very being-the idea of whom is within me- the one that has no defects and has all those perfections that I can't grasp, but can somehow touch with my thought."

questions.enonce_markdown: State the main theme and its logical articulations in the text.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Main theme.** The passage presents Descartes' proof of the existence of God from the idea of God that he finds within himself: the idea of a perfect being is a mark, like a craftsman's stamp, that the creator has set in the mind of his creature, so that the existence of this idea shows that God exists. It is the argument known as the Trademark Argument of the Third Meditation.

**Logical articulations.**
1. *Starting point:* I have within me the idea of God, which I understand as a being without defects and with all perfections.
2. *The idea is a mark of its maker:* if God created me, it is natural that he put this idea in me, as a craftsman marks his work. Being made in his image and likeness, I perceive that likeness as I perceive myself.
3. *The finite mind knows its own limits:* when I look at myself, I understand that I am incomplete, dependent on something else, and that I aspire without limit to greater and better things.
4. *Inference from lack to fullness:* I understand at the same time that the being on whom I depend has within himself all those greater things; hence this being is God.
5. *Core of the argument and conclusion:* I could not exist with the nature I have, containing the idea of God, unless God really existed. So God exists.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Explain the following:

(i) "to serve as a mark of the craftsman stamped on his work."
(ii) "By 'God' I mean the very being-the idea of whom is within me."
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) "A mark of the craftsman stamped on his work."** A craftsman often puts his signature or trademark on what he makes, so that anyone who sees the object can know who made it. Descartes uses this image for the idea of God: the idea of a perfect being is God's signature in the human mind, left there by the Creator when he made us. The mark is not something additional to the work ("not that he needed any mark other than the work itself"): the mind itself, with its idea of God, bears the likeness of its maker. So to find the idea of God in us is to find evidence of the author who put it there.

**(ii) "By 'God' I mean the very being-the idea of whom is within me."** Descartes first defines what he means by the word: God is the real being of whom he has an idea, that is, a being without defects and with all perfections, infinite, which he cannot fully grasp but can in some way reach with his thought. The sentence distinguishes the idea (a content in the mind) from its object (the being the idea is about) and means that the idea has an object, a real God, and is not an invention. It prepares the argument: the idea has so much perfection that only a really existing perfect being can be its cause.

questions.enonce_markdown: What precisely is Descartes' Trademark Argument all about?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Trademark Argument is Descartes' proof of the existence of God in the Third Meditation, which starts from the idea of God found within the thinker. Its steps are as follows.
1. I find in my mind the idea of an infinite, perfect, independent and all-powerful substance, which I call God.
2. By the causal principle that Descartes accepts, there must be at least as much reality in the cause as in its effect; so the idea, which has a very high degree of represented (objective) reality, needs a cause that has at least as much reality in fact (formal reality).
3. I am a finite, imperfect and doubting substance, so I cannot be the cause of the idea of an infinite perfection; I could not have drawn it from myself, or from the senses, or made it up from the idea of the finite.
4. Only a really existing infinite and perfect being can be the cause of this idea; so God exists.
5. The idea is God's trademark: it is innate, placed in me by the Creator, who made me in his likeness.
The argument is called a trademark argument because it treats the innate idea of God as the stamp of the maker on his work.

questions.enonce_markdown: State two reasons why the Cartesian Doubt is important.
questions.corrige_markdown:
1. *It provides a firm foundation for knowledge.* By doubting everything that can be doubted (the testimony of the senses, which sometimes deceive; the dream argument; the hypothesis of an evil deceiver), Descartes clears away prejudices and uncertain beliefs and looks for something that resists all doubt. In this way knowledge is rebuilt on a certain starting point and not on custom or authority.
2. *It leads to the first certain truth, the cogito.* The doubt itself shows that, even if I am deceived, I who doubt and think must exist: "I think, therefore I am". This is the Archimedean point from which Descartes goes on to prove the existence of God and of the external world, and it establishes the thinking self and the independence of mind.
(A further reason that is also acceptable: the doubt is methodical, a tool of the search for truth and not a sceptical end in itself, and it frees the mind from dependence on the senses and from received opinion.)

questions.enonce_markdown: What does Descartes prescribe as a formula for the attainment of truth?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Descartes prescribes the method of **clear and distinct ideas**: accept as true only what the mind perceives so clearly and so distinctly that it cannot be doubted, and withhold judgment on everything else. In the *Discourse on Method* he sets out four rules:
1. *Evidence:* never accept anything as true unless I recognise it clearly and distinctly to be so, and avoid hasty judgment and prejudice.
2. *Analysis:* divide each difficulty into as many parts as necessary to solve it.
3. *Synthesis (order):* conduct thoughts in order, beginning with the simplest and easiest to know, and rising step by step to the most complex.
4. *Enumeration:* make complete lists and general reviews so that nothing is omitted.
In the Fourth Meditation he adds that error is avoided by confining the will, in giving assent, to what the intellect perceives clearly and distinctly. Truth is attained by reason and not by the senses.

**For the argument.** It is a coherent and ingenious reasoning that relies on a causal principle which many find intuitive (an effect cannot have more reality than its cause) and on a real feature of the human mind, the idea of a perfection that exceeds it. Descartes also answers the objection that the idea of the infinite is merely the negation of the finite: he says that we understand the infinite before the finite, since to know that I doubt and am imperfect I must already have an idea of a perfection to compare with.

**Against the argument.**
1. *The Cartesian circle* (Arnauld's objection): Descartes uses clear and distinct perception to prove God, and uses God to guarantee that clear and distinct perceptions are true.
2. *The causal principle is questionable.* Empiricists, from Hume to later thinkers, hold that the idea of God can be made by the imagination by enlarging human qualities (a very wise, very good, very powerful being); the idea is then explained without a real God.
3. *Innate ideas are denied by Locke and the empiricists*, who say that all ideas come from experience; the idea of God may come from education and culture, or, as Freud and Feuerbach held, from human projection.
4. Even if the cause of the idea were a perfect being, the argument would not by itself show that this being is the God of any particular religion.

**Judgment.** The argument is historically important and shows the strength of rationalism, but it is not conclusive: it depends on premises (innate ideas, the causal principle) that are open to serious objection, and on a method exposed to the charge of circularity. It is therefore only partly tenable.
